name: Frederick Douglass
role: Abolitionist, orator, editor and US diplomat (1818-1895)
summary: Born into slavery, Douglass became the leading Black abolitionist, then a Republican supporter of the Union war, Black suffrage and civil rights. He backed women's suffrage, universal immigration rights including for Chinese migrants, and national enforcement of equal rights, and opposed Black emigration schemes.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Inferred: in 1860 he insisted free speech must not be given up to mob pressure, even for unpopular speakers, and held it as the right tyrants dread most.

limit-guns.rationale: Listed it among the grievances of Black southerners that they are denied the power to keep and bear arms.

decide-locally.rationale: In 1866 he accepted that states control their local affairs while arguing the ballot rather than federal officers would protect rights; by 1883 and 1894 he demanded national power to enforce equal rights and condemned the restoration of state sovereignty.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Pressed for federal civil rights laws, the ballot and enforcement of the amendments; he also said the negro asked only fair play, so his view on remedying past injustice as such is mixed.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Rejected limiting migration, including Chinese immigration, calling migration a right belonging 'alike to all' and defending a 'liberal and fraternal policy'.

open-borders.rationale: Asserted 'the right of migration' for the Chinese, Japanese and all others as an eternal human right and wanted 'the Asiatic' to find a home in the US; he did not call for abolishing borders as such.

revolution-justified.rationale: Praised the founders who 'preferred revolution to peaceful submission to bondage'.

right-to-secede.rationale: Called the Confederate states 'the rebel' cause and urged war against it.

political-violence-never.rationale: Urged black men to join the Union army ('Action! Action! ... Who would be free themselves must strike the blow') and praised the Revolution.

separate-church-state.rationale: Praised a government 'steadily refusing to put its sword and purse in the service of any religious creed'.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Held up the US as 'the most conspicuous example of composite nationality in the world' and wanted all races to find a home in it.

direct-action.rationale: Broke with Garrisonian abstention and disunionism in favor of voting and constitutional politics (My Bondage, ch. XXIII; Reconstruction, 1866), though he also resisted Jim Crow cars and fugitive-slave captures personally; mixed.

conscription.rationale: Condemned the July 1863 draft riots as a darker chapter of the war and used the draft to argue that Black men who bear its burdens are citizens; no general statement on conscription.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Rejected the claim that colored races are worthless or inferior, saying the answer is elevating the class deemed worthless, and that human equality rests on common nature, not racial theory.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Supported annexing Santo Domingo in 1871 as a safe alliance with a weak people, but resigned as Haiti minister in 1891 when the US sought a naval base against Haiti's wishes; mixed.

bound-labor.rationale: Condemned compelled, coerced labor: slavery and the post-war South where labor 'has been whipped, chained and degraded'.

universal-morality.rationale: Said human rights 'rest upon no conventional foundation, but are eternal, universal and indestructible'; he did not address knowability by reason in so many words.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Backed equal political rights for women and rejected the argument that long custom of male rule makes it right.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Denounced the color line and the 1883 Supreme Court decision allowing private and public exclusion of colored travelers, demanding national protection of equal access.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Described man's rule over woman as universal and sustained by long-standing custom and the belief that 'what is always was and always will be'.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: In Composite Nation he rested policy on 'the principle of absolute equality' and on 'a Government founded upon justice, and recognizing the equal rights of all men'.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Described the ideal government as resting on 'nature, reason and the regularly ascertained will of the people'.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: In My Bondage (ch. XI) he writes that good clothing and his mistress's smiles could not atone for taking his liberty, treating mastery as unfreedom even when kindly exercised.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Argued that a nation of many races and creeds founded on absolute equality gains 'peace, strength and security'; diversity was a strength to him.

death-penalty.rationale: Wikipedia's summary of his career lists abolition of capital punishment among the reform causes he took up.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Backed the Union war against the rebel states and recruited soldiers to fight the Confederacy.

character-from-environment.rationale: In My Bondage (ch. XI) he describes his kind mistress being changed by holding slaves, both of them victims of the same overshadowing evil, treating character as shaped by circumstance.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Told the African Civilization Society 'we prefer to remain in America' and, in 1879, advised freedmen to stay in the South and fight for their rights there.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Inferred: his attacks on Dred Scott and the 1883 civil rights ruling demanded courts enforce equal rights, not defer to white majorities.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Praised John Brown's courage and said force must be used against slavery, yet told Brown the Harper's Ferry plan was a perfect steel trap; evidence points both ways.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Attacked the Court's ruling that let hotel-keepers and railway conductors exclude colored people, insisting the national government must have power to forbid it.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Demanded that the Reconstruction amendments and the organic law be honestly enforced and condemned the Supreme Court for hollowing out the Civil Rights Act.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Held that the war's mission was 'the liberation of the slave, as well as the salvation of the Union', and rejected the charge that blacks themselves caused it.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Described legitimate government as claiming no higher authority than nature, reason and the regularly ascertained will of the people.

property-franchise.rationale: Wrote that every argument against a property qualification for the vote applied equally against a color qualification, and said the vote ought to be enjoyed by all citizens.

racial-franchise.rationale: Demanded the ballot for the freedman as a full citizen and condemned ballot-box stuffing and devices that cheat colored voters.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Argued that the right of migration rests not on any ethnological theory 'but upon the broad fact of a common nature. Man is man the world over.'

women-suffrage.rationale: Supported the 1848 woman suffrage resolution and in 1888 said he had long been identified with the movement and gloried in having backed it.

national-church-status.rationale: Praised a government that refuses to put its sword and purse in the service of any religious creed or family, which cuts against a privileged national church.

self-ownership.rationale: Reasoned from slavery that a man's person and the fruit of his own labor are his own.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Said there is 'nothing the matter with the negro': the nation's problem is white prejudice, and the remedy is honestly enforcing the amendments.

notes:
Full texts read: the three autobiographies, the Fourth of July speech, Composite Nation, Self-Made Men, the Constitution speech, Men of Color To Arms, Lessons of the Hour, the 1888 suffrage speech, the Nation's Problem, the Exodus paper and others. Economic and many institutional statements are null because his speeches rarely address them. Early Garrisonian disunionism and later Constitutional antislavery views differ; the mature view is used.

Merged with an independent claude-sonnet-5-5 audit: 15 answers taken from it, 26 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-sonnet-5-5 notes: Book-pass: My Bondage and My Freedom (1855) read theme by theme, then Life and Times (1881/1892) and speeches from 1852 to 1894 checked for later positions. Early Garrisonian disunionism and non-political action gave way to constitutional antislavery politics by 1851-52; the later view is used. Economic, technology, ecology and most institutional statements are null because his record does not address them.
